If Trump thinks that dropping a big bomb would allow him to declare some sort of victory in a fruitless war, he is delusional, and his other recent remarks about the war seem to prove that. Meanwhile, the economy continues to flounder, and gas prices keep going up.

items.title: Trump’s New Press Secretary Disintegrates Under Slightest Pressure
items.content_text:
White House press secretary Katie Zacharia crashed and burned Thursday as she struggled to defend pretending to be an actual attorney.

Appearing on Fox News’s Hannity, Zacharia was forced to answer for her train wreck first press briefing. “It’s been widely panned, I’m sure you’re aware. It only lasted 14 minutes. You only took three questions,” host Sean Hannity said.

Zacharia claimed that since being tapped as secretary last week, she’d been given “very little prep time” and had only received the press briefing materials earlier that morning—which is, you know, generally how the news works.

Then Hannity pressed Zacharia to respond to revelations that she lied about being an actual attorney. The former on-air legal analyst had confirmed earlier that day that she never passed the bar exam—just days after she’d told reporters that she had.

“You said you consulted with many people and they advised you that it was OK to call yourself a lawyer but not an attorney, correct?” Hannity asked.

“Correct,” Zacharia said. Hannity pointed to a CNN report that showed 15 social media posts she’d shared in which she was identified as an “attorney.”

“I think they were retweets and I corrected the record and said that [they’re] not endorsing the title, they’re retweets of a title that had been given,” Zacharia stammered. (That doesn’t quite explain why President Donald Trump would then announce that he’d appointed “an attorney” to be his new press secretary.)

“Why not just say, ‘I went to Pepperdine Law School and then took a different career path, and I took the bar once and didn’t pass it?’” Hannity asked. “Why get into this long drawn-out definition between the difference between a lawyer and an attorney, ’cause I don’t think people see much of a distinction. Why didn’t you just say, ‘I never practiced law?’”

“Well, Sean, when I moved back from the United States I didn’t retake the bar, I had four kids in six years. It was never my intent to go into the practice of law,” Zacharia said.

“When I was at—when I went to go engage in media and give legal analysis, I consulted attorneys and legal professionals as to whether or not they agreed that I could be labeled a lawyer both because I had a valid juris doctor from a good law school, a reputable law school, Pepperdine law school, and in conjunction with the fact that I did have actual, substantive legal experience.

“I wasn’t providing any legal analysis, Sean—or, I’m, excuse me, legal advice. I wasn’t being paid for legal advice, I was giving a general review of the legal circumstances surrounding it,” she said.

Trump’s new press secretary better get her story straight. At best, Zacharia wildly misrepresented her credentials—at worst, she gave unlicensed legal advice. If she can’t defend her own lies, how in the world will she ever defend Trump’s?

items.title: Transcript: Dems Will Win the House. The Senate is the Big Question
items.content_text:
This is a lightly edited transcript of the October 15 edition of Right Now With Perry Bacon. You can watch the video here or by following this show on YouTube or Substack.


Perry Bacon: Good morning. I’m Perry Bacon. I’m the host of Right Now on The New Republic. We have a great guest today. It’s G. Elliott Morris. People probably already know who he is, but anyway, he was at FiveThirtyEight and The Economist before, doing great analysis of data and politics. He’s now doing his own newsletter, Strength in Numbers. He’s also helping run a site called 50 Plus 1, which has some great forecast and modeling of the election. Elliott, thanks for joining me. Great to see you.

G. Elliott Morris: Yeah, Perry. Happy to be here as always. This morning I’m on my second cup of coffee during our call. You might see me pour a third.

Bacon: All right. So I’m going to go through a bunch of different races, because you’re the man to ask for this kind of thing. So I want to start off with the House. I’ll only ask this broad question first, which is, you’ve been discussing this a lot, but I don’t think we’ve had it on Right Now, and this is just asking very explicitly: my liberal friends, and most of my friends are liberal, are very nervous about 2016, 2020, 2024.

Their perception is the polls are always wrong and the polls are always inflating Democratic vote share, and they’re very nervous about being disappointed again. So should they be panicked by the polls showing Democrats leading by a fairly substantial margin?

Morris: This is a good question.

Bacon: Maybe panicked is—I framed the question poorly. Talk about—

Morris: No, I think you should be as panicked—so I was at an event with a senator recently, and they asked this question, “Are the polls right?”

Bacon: Like a United States senator asked people this question. That’s interesting.

Morris: Yeah. A US senator asked the polling nerds in the room, Hey, are the polls going to be right? And there were some people in the room that are like, Hey, we’ve made a lot of changes over the last couple years or the last decade. They should be more accurate than they were in 2016, for example, when they weren’t weighting by education, which was just, in hindsight, kind of a rookie error. It’s just one of those things that wasn’t necessary before, so pollsters didn’t do.

And I wasn’t super convinced by this. My response to the senator was, they’re about as good as they have been historically, which is to say you should expect them to be off by about three percentage points, potentially in every single race by about the same amount.

Which is the type of error that we would not have reacted so harshly to, first off, in a year where there’s a blowout, when it just doesn’t matter, or when people weren’t conditioned to expect so much precision from the polls.

So I think the thing that has changed over the last 15 years—and it was truer in 2016 and less so now, because there’ve been so many errors—is that people just expect the polls to be super accurate. And they’re not. But they’re not necessarily worse than they have been historically. There were some cases of some really huge errors in the 1980s. So if you want me to give some comfort to your super blue listeners, the comfort is they’re almost certainly going to win the House, and you can do a lot of things without winning the House.

Bacon: Let me stop you there for a second to ask that. Because you do these forecasts, so presumably you think the polls are not useless. So you’re saying the polls might be 3 percent off, but the forecast accounts for that, correct?

Morris: Yeah. So the reason why the forecasting is useful is that it explores what could happen if the polls are wrong. If they are off in the amount that they have been historically.

Bacon: Off in the past.

Morris: In my mind, we’re doing the hard work for you, the reader, or in this case the viewer, by taking the polls today and shifting them three points in one direction, count up the seats. Today Democrats lead in 54 states according to the polls.

If you shift all the polls three and a half points, 3.3 to be exact—that’s the historical error for Senate polling this far ahead of an election—you can get 49 seats for the Democrats if you shift in the Republican direction, or 56 for the Democrats if you shift in that direction. That is the range. Most of these outcomes include Democrats controlling the Senate, but not all of them.

Bacon: Let’s go through the details of that. Your estimate is the Democrats have a 99 percent chance of winning the House, on 50 Plus 1. The median outcome is 49 seats gained by the Democrats, so 242.

I looked up VoteHub today. They have it at 231 seats and an 84 percent chance. Split Ticket has it at 234 seats and an 89 percent chance. So in other words, the 84, 89, 99—the analysts agree the House, it would be an almost unprecedented error in forecasting and polling if—the Democrats are overwhelming favorites to win the House. Is that correct?

Morris: Yeah. And just to say, I think The Economist is at 95 and Nate Silver is at 93 or something. I don’t subscribe to Nate Silver so I can’t see, but I have someone who does subscribe tell me the number every Friday. So that’s as of last Friday. It could be even higher by now.

So it’s not hard to believe, like 90, 95, frankly not hard to believe. Democrats only need to pick up three seats. In the generic ballot today, the test of the House popular vote, they’re doing around plus eight or plus nine in terms of margin, which would be an 11 percentage point shift since 2024.

The last time there was a shift that large was 2018, and that year Democrats gained 42 seats. So they’re going to gain less because of gerrymandering. But maybe just 35. OK, they only need to gain three. So it would take a 9/11 style political event.

Bacon: We’ll pick a different analogy, but I get the point you’re making.

Morris: I know it can be toxic, but actually that was the last time—2002 was the last time the incumbent party in the White House gained seats in the House. That’s what I mean by that.

Bacon: I see. Got it.

Morris: So it would be two out of the last 100 years or so of House elections is what we’re talking about. And obviously we have a lot of leading indicators. There’s no signs of that sort of political environment. Like in 2002, it was easy to see this coming. Democrats weren’t leading by 10 points in the generic ballot.

Bacon: Senate, you have Democrats winning 71 out of 100. This is a 71 percent chance, I think, and you have a median outcome of 52 seats for the Democrats. VoteHub has it at 59 percent Democratic, likely to win 52 seats. Split Ticket at 65 percent and 52 seats as well.

So that’s around where Hillary versus Trump was. That’s in the range of Trump’s potential win in 2016 when he was the underdog. So in other words, people should not be banking on—the Republicans holding the Senate is a realistic outcome of the November elections, correct?

Morris: Yeah. The way to read the polls today is that if they have an error that is historically average, in the Republican direction, Republicans hold the Senate. If there is a larger than average miss, then Democrats might only be picking up two or three states, maybe even one. And those sort of errors happen, and they are basically impossible to predict ahead of time.

The reason I like the forecasting is that we are doing a lot of this hard number crunching for people behind the scenes to prepare optimistically, right? To prepare them for potential polling error that might happen on election day.

Instead of saying, “Just look at all these polling averages, look who’s up, look who’s down,” I think that leaves a lot of information on the table, since there’s a lot of uncertainty we can talk about with the election forecast that you can’t get by just looking at the polls. That’s the entire reason the forecasting exists in the first place.

Bacon: So the Senate, we should be looking carefully at, and that is something that, like you said, a normal polling error. I think that’s a good phrase, actually.

Morris: Yeah. And it’s not hard to see how this would happen. So Democrats are leading by three points in Texas. I think a little bit more, four points maybe, in Ohio. They’re leading by a couple of points in Maine, where Susan Collins has historically beat the polls, and they’re leading by one point in Iowa. They’re leading by two points in Kansas.

I don’t know if I believe that, but we are not in the business of putting our thumb on the table. We can come back to Kansas. So there’s one seat for Democrats that I think is a pretty sure thing. That’s North Carolina. Former Governor Roy Cooper is super popular in the state. He’s up 5.1 percent in the polls.

Bacon: One seat they’re going to flip, just to be clear what we’re talking about. Ossoff’s going to win, but one seat they’re going to flip, yeah.

Morris: So one Republican to Democratic flip. That gets them to 48, and then all these other states I’ve just listed, those are within three points. Those are within the historical average polling error for Senate races.

Don’t be surprised if the polls are wrong. They’ve been wrong before, and in this case, if they are as wrong as they have been on average historically, it means Republicans hold the Senate.

Bacon: Interesting. OK, so let’s go through some races specifically now. So I looked up Cook Political Report and went through some of their likely, toss-up, et cetera, and their breakdown. So let me go through these three. So Cook Political says likely—which, likely versus lean, we’ll come back to that. So likely Democratic Senate, Georgia, North Carolina, and they’re saying Minnesota is likely as well, but maybe not solid.

So talk about Minnesota. Do you think there’s an outcome—how likely is it? Because the Republicans are hinting Minnesota, there’s a lot of talk that the Democratic candidate is not particularly strong there. Do you see any realistic chance of an upset in Minnesota, where the Republican could win?

Morris: A lot of people tell me—

Bacon: Are you saying yes?

Morris: No, I’m not going to give you a yes or no answer, Perry. Nice try.

Bacon: Fair enough. I want to make sure—you said “Yeah,” so that’s why I was making sure.

Morris: Oh, OK. No, I’m not saying yes.

A lot of people tell me Peggy Flanagan’s a bad campaigner, she’s a bad fit for Minnesota. I think this is a lot of rationalization of the polling numbers. It is hard for me to know whether or not that’s—I don’t really think we can quantify what makes a good campaigner, a bad campaigner, very well.

So much of this is subjective. And also, it really doesn’t matter until people start counting the votes. So maybe it’s true, maybe that’s an explanation for her lagging poll numbers. I don’t really know.

The fact of the matter is, the polls in Minnesota are closer than you would expect. Peggy Flanagan’s leading her challenger, the former sportscaster there, by four points in the polls. This is a state where, in a year Democrats are leading nationally by eight or nine points, you should expect Minnesota to be two points to the left of that.

So you should expect Peggy Flanagan to be around D plus 11, and she’s at D plus four. So it is true that she’s underperforming, and that race could go the other direction.

However, what we know from studying polling accuracy historically is that usually when the polls are wrong, they err in the direction of the fundamentals. That would mean in a blue state, in a blue year, the polls have historically underestimated support for the Democrat. Or in your Kansases, your Iowas, your Ohios, your Texases, if the polls are wrong, typically in states like that, the Republican would tend to overperform.

And that’s because we have other information from the fundamentals that give us clues about elections that’s independent of the polling data. You want to average these two things together, historically speaking.

So our forecast model is around the likely Democratic zone in Minnesota. We have Peggy Flanagan at about an eight out of 10 chance. So slightly more optimistic than, to take your example, Clinton’s odds of victory in 2016. But a 17 percent chance happens one out of seven times. There’s 30 elections this year in the Senate, so it wouldn’t be totally surprising to see that race go the other way. And if it does, then the Democratic path to a Senate majority gets really hard.

Bacon: So lean—Cook Political lean Democratic, so less than likely. They have New Hampshire—

Morris: And by the way, lean means something around 70, 75 percent chance in Cook’s ratings historically. And likely is around 95.

Bacon: OK. That’s not what they say. That’s what you’ve calculated, right?

Morris: That’s what I’ve calculated based off their historical ratings. I don’t think they give the probabilities like this.

Bacon: I don’t think they say that.

Morris: Yeah, I don’t think they agree with the quantification of the ratings in general.

Bacon: They have lean, which is, like I said, less than likely, as you’re saying. Lean Democrat, New Hampshire. So do you see that as a place also where we could get an upset? What’s your sense of New Hampshire?

Morris: Yeah, New Hampshire is a weird one. The polls were really close there about a month ago, but—sorry, I’m blanking on Pappas’s first name. Help me out here.

Bacon: Chris.

Morris: It’s not Chris. Oh, are they both Chris?

Bacon: I think—

Morris: Chris Sununu is John Sununu’s brother. Yeah, Chris Pappas. I was like, surely they couldn’t both be Chris.

Bacon: Yeah.

Morris: They could. It was a really close race earlier in September, for example, back when the primary was going on. It’s possible that there were a lot of Democrats that would end up voting for Chris Pappas that were supporting his challenger, that wouldn’t admit that, and now they’ve come around.

But the race isn’t looking nearly as close as it was previously. And the quantitative forecasts like ours at 50 Plus 1 that were hedging on those close polls and saying, this state looks like a state that would be more favorable to Democrats—I think that hedging was right, and the race raters weren’t saying this race is a toss-up, I believe, even though there was a lot of conversation online about maybe New Hampshire is going to fall to John Sununu again. It doesn’t look that close.

Now, again, seven-point lead in the polls—leads of that size have evaporated with about a 5 to 10 percent chance, this close to an election. So it’s not impossible that John Sununu could win. But yeah, this is one of those states I think people got a little out over their skis on a month ago. It’s not as close as it seemed.

Bacon: So toss-up. They list seven states: Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio, Texas. So the ones I want to talk about right now are Michigan and Kansas as toss-ups. What’s your sense of Michigan and Kansas?

Morris: Michigan. If you ask someone from the Cook Political Report this question, or from election Twitter posting universe, they’re going to say, “Oh, Abdul El-Sayed is too progressive to win in Michigan,” or maybe he’s more progressive than your moderate candidate in Michigan, so he’s underperforming expectations. I think we could save the hand-wringing in the moderation versus progressive debate until the actual votes are counted and we see how much he underperforms by.

There’s also a lot of other descriptive factors about Abdul El-Sayed that might be making him underperform in Michigan. There’s other experience factors that could also be factoring in here. So I don’t want to anchor us to any particular explanation now, especially one that is exclusive of other explanations, like your first Muslim senator winning in Michigan. That seems like, maybe some white voters in Michigan might not be so happy about that. Let’s at least leave that on the table as a possibility now.

But this is slightly surprising to me in terms of the Mike Rogers of it all, rather than the Abdul El-Sayed of it all. Mike Rogers underperformed by a couple points in 2024 when he ran and lost to Elissa Slotkin.

Bacon: Let me ask you. What’s surprising is the race is close, or you’re saying that Cook is calling it close? Because those are different questions.

Morris: So it is surprising that Cook is calling it a toss-up, given the polls show consistently that El-Sayed has, I think, a three to four-point lead, four-point lead. So they’re saying, “Oh, these polls are...” The literal read of that is that they’re betting on some amount of polling bias. Which, they have their right to. Maybe they’re seeing some internal data that we’re not seeing.

But from a 30,000-foot perspective, I would have also expected Mike Rogers to be doing worse, as someone who recently lost an election in Michigan. He underperformed Donald Trump in Michigan in losing the state.

And that is a state that has been hit hard by tariffs and, just like everywhere else, by price increases and the affordability crisis that Donald Trump has publicly taken basically a lot of credit for, in pushing for inflationary policies over the last 20 months.

So if Abdul El-Sayed loses there, it’ll be a combination of factors. Maybe he was too progressive for some members of the Democrats. Maybe he was too Muslim for other swing voters. Maybe Mike Rogers did better in the debate, right? We can add up all those factors. But yeah, it’s close enough that it could go either way. That’s the state where a normal polling error means Mike Rogers wins the race.

Bacon: Kansas. I’ve not read all these polls. I’m just very dubious of calling Kansas a toss-up, but I’ll be open to your perspective, and if I’m wrong, I’m open to being told that.

Morris: Our model says Kansas is a toss-up. I wouldn’t put on the internet Perry Bacon is wrong about Kansas. You can disagree with the polling error, or you can disagree with the polls in a state that red, with that many working class white voters. You could make the case that the polls are undercounting Republicans there. My whole point is that we don’t know about that until the election.

Bacon: But your look at the data suggests it’s a toss-up, though. The polling is close, is your point.

Morris: The polling suggests a toss-up, with Hamilton—I’m just looking up our polling so I can give you the precise numbers for your audience. Hamilton leading by two points now on average against Roger Marshall. Some polls have it at one. New York Times has it tied.

Bacon: Hamilton’s the Democratic candidate.

Morris: Yeah, Adam Hamilton’s the Democrat. So, like I said, these are the types of people who haven’t been answering the polls in recent elections, so maybe those polls are wrong.

I am surprised that Cook calls it a toss-up, because the whole point behind the qualitative race handicappers is that they take a holistic view of all the indicators, that they don’t hew so closely to the polls. So that makes me think that they are seeing some other internal data, or with candidate interviews, that also suggests that the race would be close.

And typically your best predictions for elections come in averaging the polls and the handicappers and the fundamentals. In the case of Kansas, these are all suggesting basically a tied up race in an environment that’s this Democratic. So maybe it actually does make sense. This is not the type of state we would have all expected to be competitive a year ago, though. So I understand the hesitation from people, the skepticism.

Bacon: So Texas is called a toss-up here. My sense of looking at the polls—

Morris: Cook is calling it a toss-up, just to be clear.

Bacon: Toss-up. What I’m asking is, because in this case, you’re saying a three to four-point polling miss is typical. My sense is the polls are showing Talarico ahead by more than three or four points.

Are they just assuming Texas is Republican, just the way I would? Is there some reason to think this is a toss-up beyond the history of Texas? Because the data would seem to be in the Talarico-is-the-favorite zone, as far as I can tell.

Morris: Yeah, exactly. And our forecast had Texas at lean, right? A 60 percent chance for Talarico yesterday. And today it says toss-up, because he’s gone from 60 percent chance to 59 percent chance. There’s really no difference between these takes in terms of the numbers of it all.

But your read is correct. If Cook is seeing the same data we are, Talarico up three on average, and they’re calling it a toss-up still, then they are averaging it with the fundamental indicators. That would be stuff like Ken Paxton holds a statewide office. This is a state that’s really red. Maybe you would consider that Ken Paxton has been plagued by some amount of scandal, although it’s not rising to the level of, he’s sleeping with his staffers, right? The type of scandal that does typically rock the campaigns.

These recent leaks of him talking about how bad his campaign is doing does not help. You should probably not be allowing so many donors in the room with their phones at that point, I would think.

Bacon: But you’re saying that your polling average in Texas is about three, and if it’s three, then that gets in the normal polling error. That makes sense. I’ve seen polls saying the poll rates higher.

Morris: But to call it a toss-up, you have to bet on the polls being biased in the Republican direction by about that much. Which is not a bet that historically would have worked out. So Cook is saying, “We actually will take that bet. We do think the polls are maybe overestimating Talarico because of some other data we’re seeing, campaign finance, whatever.”

There is a lot of money being spent on Ken Paxton’s behalf. And you know what? People wouldn’t spend a billion dollars in elections if it didn’t matter. So maybe we can expect that to have a difference in the last two and a half weeks, three weeks, wherever we are.

Bacon: How do you see Maine?

Morris: Yeah, Maine’s great. It’s a good example of the tension where the polls and the fundamentals disagree. In Maine in 2020, Susan Collins beat the polls by about eight percentage points against Sara Gideon in that race. This is one of the larger polling errors of recent time in a Senate election.

So it’s notable that if you’re expecting that level of polling error again, the polls to underestimate Susan Collins—and she has beaten expectations four elections in a row—that’s a fair enough expectation. Let me just get to our Senate forecast here for Maine. Then you would be expecting her to be leading in the fundamentals view of the race, right?

Let’s just unpack that for a second. If Susan Collins typically beats the polls by eight points, and historically she’s beaten the average challenger by more like 12 or 13 points above what we would have expected based on how blue the state is in presidential elections, you would be expecting her to win by four or five points this year.

So the polls then showing Troy Jackson up three points, that’s an example where, contrary to in Texas or in Kansas, the fundamentals and the polls really disagree.

So like I said earlier, those fundamentals—you should expect polls typically to miss in favor of the fundamentals, for the election results to be somewhere between the polls and the fundamentals. And that argues for a more skeptical view of the surveys in Maine. So they show Troy Jackson up two points.

Maybe you can mentally adjust this in your head and say, if you’re a Democrat, always two points behind. I typically tell people just always subtract two from the side you’re betting for in the polls, and then you’re prepared for if they’re wrong. You can make your campaign decisions in the world that you’re behind, that can prepare you for victory better.

But I really have no idea on the ground. So I’ll just say a couple things about the issues. I know you have more questions. ICE and immigration have been a huge issue in Maine. Jackson has been dogging Susan Collins for her votes for ICE and DHS funding in these debates, and there’s some high-profile incidences of violence and death at the hands of ICE in Maine.

So this is one of those states where immigration is maybe more on the minds of voters than it is elsewhere. And affordability, and especially gas and diesel prices, matters in a state like Maine in the winter, where most people heat their homes with oil.

So I would expect, based on the issues, that Troy Jackson comes out ahead. The fact that it is so close suggests, maybe our storytelling about Susan Collins as the enduring moderate has some staying power in 2026.

Bacon: OK. So Cook likely Republican—I’m going to go through these three states quickly. Likely Republican: Nebraska, South Carolina, Florida. Do you think there’s any chance Democrats win, or I guess not Democrats in the case of Nebraska—is there any realistic chance Republicans lose Nebraska, South Carolina, or Florida?

Morris: Yeah, there’s a chance for sure. Our model thinks that there’s about a 20 percent chance that Democrats take either Florida or Nebraska, and maybe closer to 30 or 40 percent in South Carolina. Just based mainly on the surveys in South Carolina, that is.

And this is maybe a word about the forecasting models here. One of the reasons why the quantitative forecasts are so optimistic is that they’re simulating different elections. In one election, they take the polls and they add five points. In one simulation, they take the polls and they subtract five points for the Democrats.

Sometimes they also will explore state by state errors in the surveys. And if you do that enough, then on average in these states, South Carolina, Florida, and Nebraska, in these simulations, you should expect the Democrats to pick up one of those in many of these simulations.

I think on average these are adding about a third of a seat to the Democrats’ total. So that pushes up their expected seat number on average, which increases their probability of victory. Because it’s, oh, there’s some edge cases in these states. We don’t really know what’s going on in South Carolina. So maybe Democrats pick up that seat in this simulation.

If you do that 40,000 times, like we do at 50 Plus 1, like Nate Silver does, then these models are accounting for surprises in these edge likely seats. And so that adds to their total. Whereas if you’re just taking a straight count of the qualitative race raters, you would basically wipe all these likely Republican states off the map.

South Carolina’s a really interesting one. I don’t have to tell you, this is a really Republican state. Annie Andrews seems like a type of Democrat that might be able to win in South Carolina, and maybe one dynamic here is both of the nominees are women.

So there’s potentially less latent sexism fueling voters’ decisions in a Southern state, because both of the nominees are women. Also Lindsey Graham wasn’t exactly beloved for his support of the war in Iran at the time of his demise, and that could be weighing on his—I’m sorry, is it his sister or his sister-in-law? It’s his sister, right?

Bacon: Yes.

Morris: Yeah. It’s not implausible that in a super Democratic year where there’s a lot of anti-incumbency bias, someone like Annie Andrews could win there. I am personally, after seeing the polls, a lot less optimistic on behalf of Angie Nixon in Florida than I am for Annie Andrews in South Carolina.

Bacon: OK. So governor, Cook toss-up: Wisconsin, Georgia, Nevada, Ohio. Talk about Wisconsin and Georgia, because the sort of Twitter, Bluesky discussion assumed that Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms is in big trouble because she’s being outspent by a lot, and assumed that Wisconsin, the Democrats picked the quote unquote “normal candidate” and they’re going to be fine. So do you see Wisconsin and Georgia as toss-ups?

Morris: I see them as toss-ups. Yeah. In Wisconsin the Democrat is ahead by two points in the polls. That’s within that historical polling error range we’ve been talking about. In Georgia, it’s the opposite. Bottoms is behind by one and a half or two points in the polls.

These are both states where if the polls are wrong, they could go the other way. Toss-up seems reasonable, especially in states that are—and Georgia’s definitely to the red of the nation as a whole.

Wisconsin, at the state level, is a little redder. But a weird thing about Wisconsin is that it gets so much investment that it doesn’t tend to move as much as the overall national popular vote does. So I’m just going to say two sentences about this. In between 2020 and 2024, the national popular vote moves six points to the right.

Wisconsin moves a point and a half to two points to the right, if you’re generously rounding on Donald Trump’s behalf. And it was similar from 2016 to 2020, it moves a point, whereas the nation as a whole moves by about two and a half.

Bacon: So it’s been very divided and very polarized, or something like that.

Morris: Very divided, yeah. And it gets a lot of investment, so there’s a lot of voter contact that helps the Democrats reach the people that they’re always trying to reach, who can fall into the sort of low engagement category in other states.

So Republicans that have been talking about, “Let’s just get Trump out, and we’re going to activate all of our low turnout propensity Republicans”—there’s a lot fewer low turnout propensity Republicans, in terms of composition of the population, in Wisconsin, because it gets so much investment from the parties. The voters there are really high turnout propensity just in general.

So it’s kind of a weird state. I would expect it to be close, even in a big blue kind of year.

Bacon: Every election there is close.

Morris: Every election in Wisconsin is close. Yeah. I had the former chair of the state party, Ben Wikler, on the Strength in Numbers podcast a while ago, and he lays out a much better explanation than I’m giving you here, in terms of how the party actually makes its investments in voter contact. That explains why it is less elastic, why vote choice there is more stable, and why it’s always close, regardless of what the nation as a whole looks like.

Bacon: OK. Lean Republican governor’s races, Florida and Texas. And the reason I brought this up is because those would be earth-shattering. Like, Talarico beating Paxton is explainable in part because Paxton seems like a corrupt, crazy person. But either one of those races flipping at the gubernatorial level would be really big news on the map. How do you see those races?

Morris: I think those ratings are good. I’m from Texas, and it’s not going to be a mystery to your audience, I lean to the left. So I think that Greg Abbott has done a bad job as governor. And this isn’t super punditry, there’s some good examples of this. There’s a lot of dissatisfaction on two policies in particular, data centers and the education system, which both cross party lines.

So in the Texas education system, the public schools have been closing, which really impacts a lot of those lower engagement, maybe lower turnout propensity voters who aren’t super high income and can send their kids to—

Bacon: And he’s pushing vouchers very hard in rural—rural voters often like their schools even though they’re conservatives on other issues.

Morris: Yeah, they do like to go to public school, especially if there’s not a Christian academy in their tiny town of 2,000 people, which is where I’m from. So that is potentially an issue that crosses party lines, and it’s an incumbent performance issue.

You don’t want the schools to be closing and people to be mad at you for not having the schools open. This was a chief criticism of Joe Biden and his response to COVID, was that the schools were closed. That’s potentially bad for him.

The big one is data centers. Greg Abbott has seen how toxic the data center push has become and completely flip-flopped on this. The issues here might be enough. They might be anti-incumbency enough, anti-leadership enough, for him to not get that fourth term. And four terms in a row, that is a lot. Even in a state like Texas. I think Rick Perry only had three, although he bowed out, so maybe he’d go to four. I don’t know.

And basically the only way to get enough Republicans to vote for Gina Hinojosa, his challenger, is for that anti-incumbency bias to sway a lot of Republicans either to vote for Gina Hinojosa or to not turn out to vote.

The other factor you might ask me about next is, does Ken Paxton’s bad campaign weigh on Abbott? It’s interesting, Ken Paxton is saying that’s going the other way around, that Greg Abbott has been bad for his campaign, in some of this leaked audio, if I’m remembering correctly. It’s like a fun blame game being pushed around here by both of the Republican nominees.

It’s possible that there’s some voters who just won’t turn up at all because they don’t have a Senate candidate to vote for. I think the likelier thing is that there’s an undervote. That there’s a good number of Republicans that turn out to vote in Texas, and they vote for Greg Abbott, and he gets in, but they leave off voting for Ken Paxton, because they don’t find it morally justifiable, or for whatever reason they don’t like the guy.

This is what a lot of voters said that they would do in, I believe, a New York Times focus group of Texas last week. So there’s some anecdata that this might be brewing, an undervote in Texas.

Bacon: Last thing, I’ll make my own comment here, which is, it looks like Roy Cooper and Ossoff are going to probably win by more, and Cooper particularly is more a center moderate. He might win by more than the Democrats in Minnesota, Maine, or Michigan do. So I think you’ll hear a lot of commentary, “This proves moderation is coming.”

Morris: Oh my God.

Bacon: And you’re already seeing that.

Morris: Yeah, the groundwork is being laid for this. People are sending me stuff about this morning.

Bacon: I do want to say one thing I’ve been thinking about. I’m on the progressive side, I wouldn’t hide otherwise, so that’s part of it. But I do want to note that it looks like one of the biggest gaps is going to be between Keisha Lance Bottoms and Jon Ossoff, and Keisha Lance Bottoms is very close to Joe Biden, quintessential moderate.

So my view is, different candidates do better. Roy Cooper has been elected like 1,000 times in North Carolina. He’s a very good candidate for reasons that are not just about ideology. Keisha Lance Bottoms has the same ideology, but maybe is not necessarily as popular, has not run statewide.

So my point is only, elections are more complicated than just ideology, not that ideology might not matter. I’d be curious how you respond to that. And also, this sort of micro fixation on who won, comparing individual states and so on, is a little bit tricky. But I want to just see how you respond, and we’ll close there.

Morris: So there’s another great reason why Democrats might be doing poorly in Michigan and Minnesota. Or in—oh, the New Hampshire governor is a Republican. Kelly Ayotte, right?

Bacon: A Republican in this case, yes.

Morris: Yeah. So definitely this applies to Michigan and Minnesota, however. They have Democratic governors.

Bacon: New York too.

Morris: New York’s definitely—this also applies to New York. They have Democratic governors.

If what we’re seeing is a broad anti-incumbent backlash at the federal level, anti-Donald Trump—and this is voters are really mad about prices, about the federal government still being involved in the war in Iran—and they’re just reflecting that anger at the party in power. Who’s the party in power in Michigan and Minnesota? It’s Democrat.

So maybe I’ll put it this way. That is a potential explanation for why El-Sayed and Peggy Flanagan are doing poorly compared to expectations in Michigan and Minnesota, and why the Democratic nominee for governor of Michigan—I’m forgetting her first name. Is it James Benson, or Benson—

Bacon: It’s Jocelyn Benson.

Morris: Oh yeah, the Republican’s name is James.

Bacon: John James is the Republican. Jocelyn Benson is the Democrat.

Morris: Why she might be doing poorly compared to your expectations based on the national environment, and how left-leaning or right-leaning compared to the nation as a whole Michigan is. Actually, that race, the governor’s race, could end up being right on the dot. But that is a potential explanation.

And people have been asking about the moderation versus progressive thing for so long, because I have put myself on the side of the empirical political science on this, which is that we just don’t have enough evidence—in out of sample tests in the future—that a progressive or that a moderate would significantly outperform the average candidate that would be put up by the Democratic Party in these races.

Sure, of course you don’t want to run AOC in Kansas. That’s not my argument. But compared to the average type of candidate you might get in these places, there’s just not enough elections to really say either way, especially in our modern age of high polarization.

And what I’ve been trying to invite people to do is to see elections as products of multiple features of candidates, the way that voters see them, rather than just seeing politics in this one-dimensional moderate versus progressive, or thinking broader left versus right dynamic, that we just know from voter psychology, a lot of voters don’t possess the same lens or the same conceptualization of ideology.

Bacon: People voted for Obama and Trump in consecutive elections. That would tell you that they’re not thinking about ideology in some strict way, or even race, or even other things.

Morris: Or also that their ideology can change. That the features of ideology can change. What makes people a moderate or progressive changes over time. And just the very fact of that change means we should be less confident in our narration about, I think, why people are making their decisions and the ideological conceptualization.

But I would invite you, if Abdul El-Sayed loses, to view that loss not just as a, “Oh, he supported Medicare for All, he lost.” But like I was saying earlier, there’s a lot of other features of the man, Abdul El-Sayed, that might not be palatable to your average white Republican, potentially swing voter or low propensity voter in Michigan. And elections are multi-factor.

Bacon: That’s not reassuring either, but it is more complicated. The fact that he’s Muslim—we have some evidence that being Muslim is challenging, and that is not ideal for the country I live in, but it’s more complicated than just Medicare for All. Probably it’s more important than Medicare for All in some ways.

Morris: It’s also just truer. It’s just truer to the voter psychology and how voters are seeing these candidates. If you watch Fox News, the narration about Abdul El-Sayed is scary. His photo’s always up there. He’s generally brown looking, but they make him look super brown compared to really white Mike Rogers right next to him.

Bacon: It’s not a fixation on, Pete Buttigieg supports a public option and El-Sayed wants Medicare for All. It’s not really in that nuanced way.

Morris: Yeah, the way that you and I are placing candidates potentially on the left-right spectrum, we just know that’s not how many voters are engaging in politics. Actually, most voters.

I will leave you with one point of data, which is, in a survey that I have yet to release, about 30 percent of the public cannot name the party that is currently in control of the House of Representatives, and cannot say which party is the more conservative political party in America. They pick the wrong option. They either say Democrats are in charge or Democrats are more conservative.

Bacon: You said 30 percent of likely voters?

Morris: That’s just a political knowledge thing.

Bacon: It’s just a political knowledge thing. The likely voters number probably is better on that than this, which is all people, right? So many people don’t vote in this country.

Morris: This is all people. Yeah. Maybe the likely voters have slightly higher levels of political knowledge. We can check that. But there’s still going to be a significant number of people out there who lack these key concepts that we are all using in the commentariat to explain politics. So a lot of voters don’t view politics in that way.

Bacon: Elliott Morris, great to see you. Congratulations. MSNBC is going to start using some of your data and analysis on their website and on television. That’s a great coup for you.

Morris: MS Now.

Bacon: Yeah, MS Now. Glad you corrected me there. And also I encourage people to subscribe. It’s Strength in Numbers. It’s one of the best Substack newsletters that I can think of. I learn a lot from it. I encourage other people who do Substack letters to be as good and add information, not just opinions, the way Elliott does. So congratulations on all your work, and great to see you.

Morris: Oh, thanks, Perry.

Bacon: Bye-bye.

items.title: Why the Democrats Might Not Flip the Senate
items.content_text:
You can watch this episode of Right Now With Perry Bacon above or by following this show on YouTube or Substack. You can read a transcript here.

What happens if polls are overstating Democratic support, as they have in recent elections? Even if polls are fairly biased against Republicans, Democrats will flip the House, elections expert G. Elliott Morris says in the latest episode of Right Now. Democrats have such a large lead in the U.S. House generic ballot and need to gain control of such a smaller number of seats (three) that a Democratic House majority is virtually guaranteed, he argues. But Republicans have a very realistic chance of holding onto the Senate if the polls are off by a few points, according to Morris. Republican chances are particularly good in Iowa, Kansas, and Texas in such a scenario. Morris also discussed why election forecasts like the ones he does are better at projecting election results than polls alone. And he cautioned against interpreting results only through an ideological lens, arguing for example that Abdul El-Sayed’s Muslim faith may hurt him with Michigan voters more than the candidate’s support of Medicare for all. Morris is the author of the newsletter Strength in Numbers and also helps run the elections website FivePlusOne.

items.title: Transcript: Fox News Poll Shocker Is an Absolute Disaster for Trump
items.content_text:
The following is a lightly edited transcript of the October 16 episode of the Daily Blast podcast. Listen to it here.


Greg Sargent: This is The Daily Blast from The New Republic, produced and presented by the DSR Network. I’m your host, Greg Sargent.

The new Fox poll is absolutely disastrous for Donald Trump. It has fresh data on his dropping approval, on the widening Democratic lead in the battle for the House, and many other things. But what if the polls are wrong? Republicans are betting on this, and there’s now a lively debate about it underway in polling circles that can’t be ignored.

So we’re going to work through both the Fox poll and the debate over polling accuracy with Natalie Jackson, a polling expert who has her own firm, Centerline, and just wrote about the topic well, as a columnist for National Journal. Natalie, thanks so much for coming on.

Natalie Jackson: Thanks for having me.

Sargent: So just to establish something quickly: in your piece, you say that Democrats will win the House. You’re treating that as a foregone conclusion, not really in doubt, and that the only big question is whether Democrats have a big year or a really big year, as you put it, the latter meaning they win the Senate. Is that basically where we are?

Jackson: I think so, because it just takes so few seats to flip the House that it’s hard to imagine that not happening in this environment. Mike Johnson has to keep hope alive for Republicans, but the only way Republicans hold the House is if everything we know about this election cycle is absolutely, disastrously wrong. And that’s not happening.

Sargent: Right. You’re essentially saying that for Democrats to not have a pretty good night, at minimum, you’d need, like, a major systemic error that reaches into every corner of what we know right now, right?

Jackson: Right. We would need at least something like a 10-point error on the generic congressional ballot. We would need Trump’s approval reality to be far different than it is. It would just be a massive upset of everything we think we know.

Sargent: Right. So Fox News just dropped this poll that neatly underscores everything you’re saying here. The top lines are that he’s at a record-low approval of 36 percent, 74 percent rate the economy negatively, and Democrats lead by nine points in the generic ballot matchup, 54 to 45. If that proves correct, Natalie—and we don’t know that it will, which we’ll get into—but if it were, that would be the stuff of a wave election, right?

Jackson: Yes. This is kind of what I put in the good night. The really good night, I think, depends on the Senate polling, which I’m sure we’ll get into.

Fox’s numbers match up with mine. I ran a national poll just a couple of weeks ago. I had 35 percent approval among registered voters, eight-point Democratic advantage. So Fox is right there in line with what I’m finding and with what really everyone is. I believe the averages right now are around a nine percent Democratic advantage.

Sargent: Exactly. I mean, the Fox poll is in line with the New York Times poll, which is another gold-standard poll. It had Democrats leading by eight points in the generic ballot matchup.

And all the polling averages that you can look at, whether it’s Nate Silver or FiftyPlusOne, you find the generic ballot matchup to be at around eight or nine points, or somewhere in the middle there. I mean, that’s where we are right now, right?

Jackson: Absolutely. That is just what reality looks like. Nobody really disagrees with that.

Sargent: Well, OK, a little more from the Fox poll. It’s incredible stuff. Trump’s approval among independents is 21 percent, with 78 percent disapproving. Among Latinos, his approval is 21 percent, with 79 percent disapproving. He’s even underwater with non-college whites, which are critical to his base, and that’s at 44 percent to 55 percent.

Natalie, this is historically bad stuff. I mean, it does rival some of the worst presidential performances in the history of modern polling, does it not?

Jackson: It does. The only other president besides Trump in his first term that even comes close to this is George W. Bush when he was leaving office, really 2006 on. But he did not see numbers quite this low.

The averages were in the upper 30s, and the same with Trump’s first term. He did not really go below the upper 30s until January 6. And now we’re seeing numbers that rival, and even in a few cases go lower than, his post–January 6 numbers.

Sargent: Yeah. I mean, he is now rivaling the aftermath of January 6, and that’s just an incredible thing, considering that he essentially encouraged a violent attack on the seat of government.

But I want to point this out, too, as well. It looks like Trump’s approval is really translating directly into the generic ballot matchup as well. Democrats lead among Hispanics by 69 to 31, and among independents by 62 to 36. Democrats are in the 60s with Latinos and independents. And Democrats are doing better than usual with non-college whites. They’re at 44 percent to the GOP’s 55 percent.

Natalie, I think you can see a Democratic coalition kind of forming there. It includes winning back a ton of the Hispanics they lost to Trump in 2024, doing very well with independents, and keeping Republican margins down with blue-collar whites and rural whites as well.

That’s the recipe that they’re going to need in some of these tough states and districts, especially ones that Trump won by high single digits or even double digits. Your thoughts on all that?

Jackson: Right. The coalition that seems to be coming together is reminiscent of what we saw in 2020, when Biden won. We saw heavily Democratic Hispanics, heavily Democratic independents. It’s a really similar outlook. And absolutely keeping those margins down in the rural areas, among the non-college voters. That’s what Democrats have to do.

The issue that I would point to is they have to be able to do it long term. This is great for Democrats for 2026. But what we’ve learned in the last few election cycles is that Hispanics are really dealigning. They’re not really that attached to either party. It used to be a more reliable Democratic core.

Now, especially among the younger generations—which Hispanics are, they do tilt younger than the rest of the population—they are not attached to either party. And they are also very heavily affected, directly affected, by the economy, by virtue of where they live, the types of industries they’re in. And so this is a group that’s going to swing, and we’re seeing a really hard swing against Trump.

Sargent: I mean, it’s going to be a big challenge to try and lock down some of these demographics over the long term. So you’re absolutely right about this.

I want to get at what the Fox poll shows about the economy as well. Donald Trump’s at 22 percent to 77 percent on inflation. Twenty-two percent on what’s clearly the biggest issue on the minds of voters right now. That’s barely more than one out of five that approve.

And by the way, Fox also breaks out non-MAGA Republicans versus MAGA Republicans, and on his overall approval, he’s actually underwater with non-MAGA Republicans. That’s 47 to 53. Those are GOP voters.

And I’ve got to think that looms large in some of these Senate races where Democrats have to win some Republican voters. These are states where Trump prevailed by double digits. And the only way Democrats can get there is by winning a chunk of Republicans. So if you’ve got non-MAGA Republicans disapproving of Trump, there’s a path for them, right?

Jackson: There is a path. The approval numbers are one good indicator. Democrats really need two things to happen with these non-MAGA Republicans. They need them to stay home—some portion of them just don’t show up to vote. The other thing is they need them to be not super attached to the Republican Party.

There’s a contingent of Republicans that is very unhappy with Donald Trump. But on the other hand, they would—I’ve heard this said on cable news a couple of times—they would rather put their face in a wood chipper than vote for a Democrat. So it’s really a complicated picture, and we just don’t know what choice those non-MAGAs are going to make.

Sargent: Absolutely. Well, let’s get into your piece on how to understand the debate over whether the polls might be wrong. And again, we stress that’s always possible. The data could be wrong.

As you write, the big question is whether the polls are undercounting Republicans who aren’t that ginned up to vote, but might still end up turning out anyway and voting Republican. And maybe pollsters aren’t reaching those people.

But a lot of pollsters have taken steps to try to correct for this problem. Can you just walk us through what those steps are?

Jackson: Yes. So, brief background: In 2016, in key states, polls underestimated Trump support. Trump ended up winning. In 2020, we thought Joe Biden was going to win very easily. It turned out polls underestimated Trump even more broadly that year. Biden still won, but it took us four days to learn that after the election. It was so close.

In 2024, things were generally better. There was a slight overestimate for Harris winning. But the track record is that pollsters struggle with Trump support. It’s been better in midterms, with lower turnout different electorate.

But what we’ve done in the meantime is, we weight our data to education now. So that might seem like something fairly obvious, but it was not a practice that pollsters did before, because we didn’t have a precise number for the number of people with college degrees in the electorate.

So without a solid benchmark, we didn’t weight to it. That used to not matter, but people have polarized by education. College-educated people are more likely to be Democrats now, non-college more likely to be Republican. And so if we miss the balance on education, which we were doing, it skews toward one party or the other, and it was skewing toward Democrats.

We also started weighting more on partisanship and partisanship indicators. Some pollsters will use the prior vote. So they’ll ask, for example, who did you vote for in the 2024 election? And then they’ll make sure they have the proper number of people who voted for each candidate.

That’s tricky for a midterm, because your midterm electorate is very different. It works well when you have Trump versus Biden part two, or Trump versus Harris, who is essentially a representative of the Biden administration.

So we’ve done a lot of adjusting to the methods behind polling. There is an element that we’re always fighting the last battle, because we don’t know what is missing or what might be going on until the election happens.

Sargent: Well, OK. So looking at some of the polls that we consider to be high quality, like the Fox poll or the New York Times poll—they’re doing this weighting stuff, and they’re also trying to correct for the problem of not reaching Republicans. Those two things are related, I get that.

Can you talk about the fact that Fox and the New York Times are taking steps here to do what you’re talking about? Like, do you feel reassured? Can we look at their data and say they’re really trying to get to the right place on it?

Jackson: I believe they are. Fox and the New York Times are among the top media pollsters out there, the top any pollsters out there, honestly. They are very careful to make sure that they speak to enough Republicans. What I was talking about was adjusting the data on the back end, but those adjustments only go so far if you don’t talk to the right mix of people in the beginning.

And so one of the things that Fox and the New York Times do very well is they make sure on the front end that they have talked to a good mix of people. And those things take effort and they take money, which is why a lot of pollsters don’t do it. But these two are very reputable.

Sargent: Right. Fox and the New York Times both have the money. They are putting the resources in. It would be really, really a disaster for Fox to undercount Republicans, I think, given obvious reasons like who their audience is. And the fact that they’re constantly attacked by Donald Trump, by the way, I think that actually is a factor that could be playing in favor of accuracy.

Fox knows that they’re really on the hook big time if they screw this up. So they’re really going to put in the effort to get to those Republican voters, aren’t they?

Jackson: They are. And I have tremendous respect for Fox’s polling team, because you can imagine the internal and external pressures that they feel to show numbers that look better for Republicans than what they’re showing right now.

Sargent: I mean, Trump calls for the firing of the Fox pollsters pretty much every day at this point. Let me ask you, there’s also a scenario where Democrats could be undercounted. How would that happen?

Jackson: It’s always possible that error runs in either direction, you know? So, in our adjusting and trying to make sure that we’re getting enough Republicans, there’s always the possibility that we’re adjusting too much.

That’s kind of the thing that we don’t know: do these Republicans actually stay home? Are we going through all these hoops trying to get them to answer the surveys, and then they don’t actually vote? That would be where error would come from, making Democrats have an even better year than what we’re looking at.

Sargent: And is it possible that pollsters could somehow miss the level of energy among Democrats? Like it’s not an exact science to figure out how to screen the polling questions to try to be sure that the people who say they’ll vote are actually going to vote. Right? And so is there a scenario where you kind of undercount the number of Democrats who are actually going to show up? Is that a possibility?

Jackson: It absolutely is. We are trying to guess who’s going to vote. This is the only time that we don’t know who we need to talk to for sure. If we’re talking to registered voters, great, we know who that is. We can take a good sample of that. All American adults, great. We know who they are. We know who we need to talk to.

Likely voters don’t exist as a principle. The election hasn’t happened yet. So we are trying to cobble together several other things that predict how people vote. Some of that comes from using actual vote history. A lot of pollsters use the voter file and get their respondents’ information off of the voter file, which obviously tells you whether they voted or not the last time, the last few elections.

Some of us aren’t using voter files. So we ask a series of questions. How likely are you to vote? Some people say I’m certain to vote. Some say I’m probably going to vote. Very few will tell you straight up, I am not going to vote.

So that makes it tricky in a midterm, where turnout’s likely to max out 50, 55 percent usually. We know when we get 70, 80 percent of people saying they’re going to vote that it’s overshooting somehow. So when we try to cut that down and make it look more like the electorate, it is possible to trim too many Democrats out.

Sargent: That is just fascinating stuff. All right, just to wrap this up. What’s your best guess as to the range of outcomes in terms of polling error here? Is it your sense that the polls that we’re seeing now are pretty close to accurate?

Jackson: I think what we’re seeing from places like Fox and the New York Times are pretty accurate. I think some are kind of out there. I am less concerned about the House generic ballot. I think, you know, at most we’re looking at maybe two points, two to three points, in either direction.

Some of the Senate polling I’m a little more concerned about. Some of the specifics of each state are a little bit harder to deal with. Some of the polling that we have is not very high quality. So I do think there’s potential to see two to four points, maybe even more, in some of these Senate races off of where the polls are.

Sargent: And obviously those could flip the races in one direction or another. It looks to me as if the eight-to-nine-point generic ballot matchup kind of lines up with what the Senate polls are saying, because if you get to eight or nine points in the generic ballot matchup, you’re probably winning a bunch of those Senate seats in even Trump double-digit territory, right?

Jackson: Probably. I worry a little bit about some of the specifics in these states, and the candidates, and just the little things that can come into play in an individual environment. But overall, yes, things are very good for Democrats. And no one is arguing that Republicans are going to come out of this ahead.

Sargent: Natalie Jackson, thank you so much for all that. It’s really fascinating. Thank you so much for coming on.

Jackson: Thanks.

items.title: Will Democrats Learn the Wrong Lesson From a Blue Wave?
items.content_text:
The Democrats are poised to win big in next month’s elections. That’s great news because it will give the party enough congressional seats to rein in President Trump in Washington and enough gubernatorial and state legislative seats to blunt the mini-Trumps in red states and pass good policies in blue ones. But we shouldn’t necessarily interpret a sweeping Democratic victory as voters embracing liberalism or completely repudiating MAGA and Donald Trump.

Why not? Because voters these days, both in the United States and abroad, just seem angry at whoever is in charge and eager to toss them aside. Incumbent parties and heads of states across the world are losing popularity and elections, whether they are leftist, center-left, center-right, or far right. That includes places where the economy is fairly good and the leader isn’t corrupt or inept like Trump. So Americans may hate Trump and the GOP simply because they are the incumbent party right now but be willing to return Republicans to power immediately after the next Democratic presidential victory. Democratic leaders should not treat the 2026 results as an indication that they have figured out American politics. Instead, they should continue looking for a political program that will keep voters in their fold even when Democrats are the incumbent party.

When Kamala Harris lost in 2024, it was part of a global trend of voters rejecting incumbent parties. From 2021 to 2024, incumbent leaders were defeated in 40 of the 54 elections in Western democracies, according to Harvard political scientist Steven Levitsky. In 2024 alone, 80 percent of incumbent parties in democracies lost seats or lost vote share compared to the prior election, according to an analysis from FiveThirtyEight. That included incumbent parties in Japan, Botswana, South Africa, Senegal, Sri Lanka, and many countries in Europe.

We don’t have such sweeping data yet for 2025–2026. But anecdotally, the trend seems to be continuing. Incumbent parties have lost five of the seven national elections in the last two years in Latin America, according to an analysis from scholar Daniel Schteingart. Brazil’s leftist Workers Party seems likely to be the sixth incumbent party defeated, with its candidate, incumbent President Lula da Silva, trailing in the polls ahead of the October 25 runoff there. In Europe, ruling parties in France (center), Germany (center-right), Spain (left), and numerous other nations are sagging in polls. Britain’s center-left Labor Party ousted its leader, Keir Starmer, after the party’s poll numbers plunged. Hungary’s Fidesz, led by Trump ally Viktor Orbán, lost power in April.

In the United States, the anti-incumbent trend arguably started well before the pandemic. Since Barack Obama’s 2012 win, every subsequent U.S. congressional and presidential election has been a rejection of the party occupying the White House.

I would love to think that American voters are simply punishing the GOP this fall for Trump’s authoritarianism, the reckless tax cuts for the rich adopted by the president and Republicans in Congress, the unnecessary war in Iran that has resulted in sky-high energy prices, and the numerous other misdeeds and mistakes of Trump and his allies. But the political scientist part of my brain would say that the Republicans were essentially doomed in the 2026 midterms the moment Trump was declared the winner in 2024. It seems like everybody everywhere just hates incumbents these days.

That makes interpreting the 2026 elections here in the United States very tricky. I suspect some voters are turning from Trump due to his actions. Some of them might appreciate the Democrats’ new focus on affordability and the young, charismatic candidates that the party is running, such as Texas’s James Talarico. But I worry that Democrats have largely just captured (and stoked) anti-incumbent sentiment by blasting Trump and Republicans for high gas prices and other societal problems. Voters here and abroad seem to be willing to blame everything on their country’s head of state.

If I’m right, Democrats are in trouble the moment they win the presidency again—even if the GOP remains antidemocratic and radical. After all, Americans, frustrated with the incumbent party, sent Donald Trump of all people back to the White House in 2024. Right now, a speaker of the House in 2031 even more conservative than Mike Johnson and another Trump-like president taking office in 2033 seems entirely possible.

Therefore, it’s imperative, with the 2028 primary about to launch, that Democratic operatives and officials start considering, “How can an incumbent president/party remain popular?” Liberal egalitarian multicultural democracy depends on pro-democracy parties here and abroad figuring this out. I’m not sure about the answer. Watching Lula, Joe Biden, Starmer, Emmanuel Macron, and other leaders, I doubt that either the left’s strategy (focus on economic policy for the working class) or the center-left’s (break with minorities and marginalized groups on some issues, economic policy for the working class, economic growth) are sufficient. My thesis is that it’s some combination of economic policy for the working class, a charismatic leader, and relentless, savvy use of media and messaging. I suspect that Democratic officials should spend less time studying Bill Clinton’s and Barack Obama’s decades-old political wins and more on the popularity of Zohran Mamdani and Mexico’s Morena Party.

But I’m less sure of the solution than the problem. It’s good that this incumbent American president is unpopular, but scary and dangerous that these days it seems like all incumbent presidents everywhere are unpopular. I’m very glad America will likely have a blue wave next month. But our democracy won’t be secure until we have a blue wave while a Democratic president is in the Oval Office.

items.title: The Supreme Court Is Leaning Toward a Digital Privacy Victory
items.content_text:
The Supreme Court appeared likely to side with a customer who invoked a semi-obscure federal law to sue Paramount for sharing his personal information with Facebook, during oral arguments on Wednesday, though multiple justices signaled that they might constrain such lawsuits in future cases.

The case, Salazar v. Paramount Global, has significant potential implications for targeted digital advertising and its long-term viability. If the high court concludes that the Video Privacy Protection Act, or VPPA, forbids companies from sharing or selling online video viewers’ personal information without their consent, it could unsettle one of the primary revenue generators for some major websites.

Congress enacted the Video Privacy Protection Act, or VPPA, in response to a subplot of the Robert Bork confirmation hearings in 1987. The Senate rejected Bork’s nomination to the Supreme Court after intense scrutiny of his stances on issues such as a constitutional right to privacy, a concept that Bork had often criticized. Michael Dolan, a reporter at The Washington City Paper, asked Bork’s local movie-rental store for a copy of the movies Bork had rented there as a commentary on his views on privacy.

The store’s manager provided it without qualification. The rental history contained nothing salacious or unusual—Bork had a taste for middlebrow fare and period dramas—and played no role in the confirmation battle. But it still prompted Congress to prevent similar disclosures in the future without the customer’s consent. Lawmakers last updated the law in 2013 to reflect the emergence of Netflix and streaming services.

At issue in this particular case is whether the law’s language covers the underlying acts. Michael Salazar, the plaintiff, received a subscription through a newsletter to a college sports website, where he viewed videos about college football. Paramount, the website’s operator, installed tracking software on its web pages known as a “pixel” that logged Salazar’s personally identifiable information and automatically shared it with Facebook.

Salazar argued that this violated the VPPA, which allows “consumers” to sue “video tape service providers” for disclosing their “personally identifiable information” to third parties without their consent. The law allows individual plaintiffs to obtain up to $2,500 in damages for the violation. Given how ubiquitous digital tracking software and targeted online advertising have become, those numbers can add up fast for businesses.

His lawsuit failed in the lower courts because they concluded that Salazar did not meet the definition of a “consumer” for VPPA purposes. The law defined a consumer as someone who obtained “goods and services from a video tape service provider,” by which the lower courts concluded that Congress meant only “audiovisual goods or services.” Salazar appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing that the law as written applies to any goods or services from a provider.

Some justices appeared to favor the lower courts’ narrower interpretation. “Wouldn’t it be natural to think that goods or services from a video tape service provider would be video-related services?” Justice Clarence Thomas asked Josh Hammack, who represented Salazar. Hammack argued that other portions of the law’s language indicated that the law’s scope was meant to be broader than that.

Justice Samuel Alito also suggested at one point that the law’s scope was limited to forms of technology that are no longer in widespread use. “It is not similar in the sense that you go to a Blockbuster store and get a VHS tape,” he told Hammack.

Other justices appeared to take Paramount’s concerns seriously about the impact on internet businesses and advertising, but saw opportunities to address them in future cases. Justice Brett Kavanaugh and some of his colleagues pointed out that other questions, such as what counts as “personal identifying information” or a “video tape service provider,” might still tip in Paramount’s favor in later litigation.

“So how do we think about, you know, the sky-is-falling concern in the [friend-of-the-court] briefs—and it’s part of your brief—when there are these two other arguments that you may prevail on?” Kavanaugh asked Paul Clement, who argued on Paramount’s behalf. “And why shouldn’t we just follow ‘consumer’ as written and worry about that in a future case?”

Among Clement’s concerns in response was that, in the meantime, websites would be forced to obtain consent in cases where they might not need to do so in the future. This did not appear to persuade some of the justices. “Going forward, you have two very simple solutions,” Justice Elena Kagan explained. “One is to get consent. Easy enough. People do it every day. And the other is to stop selling people’s private information. Take your pick.”

“Yeah, or put everything behind a paywall,” Clement countered. “That would be great.”

“What’s the problem with not disclosing private video views?” Justice Sonia Sotomayor chimed in. “I mean, it’s a business for you, and it might end your business if you don’t want to get consent, but if you want to stay in the business, get consent, or just don’t do it. Other than that, you have created a business model that might contradict the law, because we still have a lot of open issues, what’s the problem?”

Clement disputed the idea that user consent would be easy or clean-cut to obtain, noting that other lawsuits have challenged the validity of it once given. Again, the justices seemed unpersuaded. “Well, that’ll always be the argument,” Kavanaugh countered. “But it seems, just technologically, isn’t it pretty easy for you all to obtain consent going forward? It’ll be a little more hassle for all of us, but …”

“For everyone,” Clement replied. “It’s just one of those cookies boxes that comes up, right?” Kagan interjected. “Yeah,” Kavanaugh added. “Wouldn’t you do it the exact same way?” Kagan offered. “I mean, we do that a thousand times a day.” Clement, at this point outmaneuvered, fell back to other arguments instead, urging the justices not to decide the case “on the assumption that consent is absolutely easy.”

One potential wrinkle for both sides is the question of whether Salazar had standing to bring the lawsuit in the first place. Paramount argued in the district court that he didn’t but abandoned that line of attack on appeal. “But, you know, the funny thing about standing arguments, you can’t really drop them,” Clement noted. Since a court’s jurisdiction is always essential to deciding a case, it can’t be forfeited by one side.

Justice Amy Coney Barrett pressed both sides on whether there was a standing issue here, with some friend-of-the-court briefs suggesting that the “pixel” tracking technology did not share what the law would understand to be “personally identifying information.” Clement did not make that argument himself, but he said he would be willing to submit additional briefs on the question if the justices were interested.

None of the other justices asked specifically about standing, and the case appeared to be headed toward a resolution on the merits. If the justices ultimately punt on this case, the recent surge in VPPA-related litigation means that the court will almost certainly address its scope and application for the modern internet at some future date. If no punt is forthcoming, a decision is expected by the end of June.

items.title: Watching Musk Feels Like Being Trapped in a Simulation
items.content_text:
Musk, Alex Gibney’s latest documentary, is nearly four hours long with a ten-minute intermission, which is surely more time than any well-adjusted person wants to spend thinking about Elon Musk. It’s to Gibney’s credit as a master storyteller and an experienced chronicler of elite malfeasance in films like Going Clear and Enron: The Smartest Guys in the Room that Musk engages and rivets throughout, even if it left me wanting both a shower and a drink.

Musk declined to be interviewed for the film. Instead he called Gibney a “douche” on the social media platform formerly known as Twitter, which Musk acquired for $44 billion in 2022 and promptly set about ruining. Gibney could have just relied on the abundant existing footage of his subject, but he went a step further, asking his research team to set up a database of all of Musk’s recorded interviews and then creating a computer-generated Musk avatar who appears to be responding to an interviewer using real statements Musk has made. It’s an unsettling gimmick, and would be objectionable in any other context, but it works here; as Gibney notes, Musk has repeated for years the popular theory that what we experience as real life is most likely a computer-generated simulation, essentially a videogame. Gibney makes this conceit literal throughout, portraying Musk as he sees himself—as the main character in a simulated digital environment in which other people are “non-player characters,” or NPCs, to be acted upon without conscience or scruple. It’s a sociopathic worldview, and what makes Musk so effective is that by the end of it, you feel as though you’ve personally been trapped in Musk’s simulation. And, well, aren’t we all?

Gibney portrays Musk as he sees himself—as the main character in a simulated digital environment in which other people are “non-player characters.”

We glimpse reality through more than a dozen unsimulated interview subjects, ranging from tech journalists (Kara Swisher, Wired’s Katie Drummond and Zoë Schiffer) to former business partners (Tesla co-founder Martin Eberhard, SpaceX co-founder Jim Cantrell) to former paramours and mothers of Musk’s many children (ex-wife Justine, the right-wing social media influencer Ashley St. Clair) to former government officials (Joe Biden’s USAID chief Samantha Power, Barack Obama’s deputy NASA administrator Lori Garver) to immediate family members (Musk’s brother, mother, and father). Most of the information Gibney presents in Musk has been previously reported, though it’s illuminating to see it all laid out here; what original revelations there are come from getting to know the various people Musk has collected, used, and discarded on his way to becoming the richest person in history.

The portrait that emerges is of an empty, hateful, emotionally stunted man whose two superpowers are shameless self-promotion and a remarkable ability to hack weaknesses in the regulatory state. These are both talents Musk shares with his erstwhile ally Donald Trump, of course, but Trump does have one other thing going for him: his undeniable borscht belt charisma. As awful as Trump is, it’s not hard to see how he won over a significant swath of the American electorate, and analogous right-wing populists have enjoyed similar success in other democratic systems around the world. Musk, by contrast, has always been a try hard, a loser at his core no matter how often he wins.
